raw_response:
I am seventy years old. I have farmed these fields in Quzhou County since I was a young man, and my father before me. I only finished primary school, but I know this land and its seasons better than any book. I have about eight mu of good flat land — not too much, because I am getting older and my back is not what it used to be, but enough to feed my household and sell a little at the market.

This year, like every year, I will grow **winter wheat** and **summer maize** in rotation on the same eight mu. That is what every household in my village does. The wheat goes in after National Day, around early October, and comes off in early June. As soon as the wheat straw is cleared, I plant the maize — no time to waste, because the frost will come by mid-October. I do not gamble with new crops like vegetables or stevia; they need too much tending and too many pesticides, and at my age I cannot crawl around the fields like that. Wheat and maize have buyers who come right to the village, so I know I can sell.

For **seed**, I buy improved varieties from the supply shop in town. For wheat I use something like Luyuan 502 or Jimai 22 — these are the kinds my neighbors use, and they resist lodging better than the old traditional seeds. For maize I buy Denghai 605 in packages. I do not save my own seed anymore; the hybrid seed gives much better yield, and the shopkeeper tells me which number is good this year.

For **fertilizer**, I follow what I have always done. Before wheat sowing, I spread compound fertilizer with the rotary tiller — about 100 jin per mu of the special blend, plus some ammonium bicarbonate for nitrogen. I topdress once more in spring when the wheat greens up. For the maize, I put down less compound fertilizer at sowing and maybe one more round when it is knee-high. I do not measure in kilograms of pure nutrient; I measure in bags and jin. But if you convert it, my wheat gets roughly 35 jin of pure nitrogen worth, 22 jin of phosphate, and 9 jin of potash per mu. The maize gets a bit less because the wheat has already fed the soil.

**Tillage**: I rotary-till the field before wheat sowing to break up the stubble and make a fine seedbed. For maize, I do not plough again — there is no time between wheat harvest and maize sowing, and the neighbors all say no-tillage works fine if you clear the straw. So I sow the maize directly into the wheat stubble field.

**Irrigation**: I have a well and I irrigate by flooding the borders. Wheat needs four good irrigations — one at sowing if it is dry, one at green-up in March, one at jointing, and one at filling. Maize only needs two: one right after sowing to help it emerge, and one at the big喇叭口 stage when the tassels are forming.

**Pesticides**: I spray herbicide once for each crop to keep the weeds down, and insecticide when I see aphids or corn borers. Wheat sometimes needs a fungicide if the weather is wet and rust appears, but usually I get by with about three sprays total for wheat and two or three for maize. I mix the tanks myself; the shop tells me the ratio.

I expect my wheat to yield about 1,050 jin per mu and the maize about 1,100 jin per mu. These are honest numbers — not the highest in the village, but I am old and I do not chase records. I just want a reliable harvest.
